summary: This work demonstrates an on-FPGA calibration and benchmarking workflow for superconducting qubits that achieves millisecond time-to-decision by co-locating pulse generation, data acquisition, analysis, and feedback on the control hardware. The workflow introduces analytical decay estimation (ADE) and sparse phase estimation (SPE) methods that enable rapid extraction of $T_1$, readout parameters, pulse amplitudes, and gate fidelities while operating a flux-tunable transmon in a closed-loop recalibration protocol over 6 hours.
motivation: Superconducting qubit parameters drift on sub-second timescales, but conventional calibration workflows suffer from millisecond-scale communication latency when offloading data to a CPU for analysis, making them fundamentally mismatched to environmental dynamics and unable to track coherence fluctuations of $T_1 = 14.5$–$27.5$ μs observed in real devices.
method: The authors implement on-FPGA versions of calibration primitives using sparse sampling ($n=3$ points) with closed-form analytical estimators: ADE extracts exponential decay rates via a SPAM-independent formula, and SPE estimates phase corrections from sinusoidally-varying signals. Additional primitives use on-FPGA implementations of Nelder–Mead optimization (readout tuning in 100 ms) and golden-section search (spectroscopy in 39 ms), all executing within the 25 ms LAN round-trip latency baseline.
result: On-FPGA recalibration achieves $T_1$ estimation in 10 ms, $\pi$-pulse amplitude optimization in 1 ms, and Clifford randomized benchmarking in 107 ms. Over 6 hours with 74,525 recalibration cycles, continuous feedback yields a 6.4% reduction in average gate infidelity ($\epsilon_g$) relative to static calibration; correlation analysis shows recalibration suppresses gate-error coupling to detuning and amplitude drift while preserving correlation to instantaneous coherence.
